skeleton: The network shows bottleneck pressure: {anomaly_count} edge{anomaly_plural} or node{anomaly_plural} sit above their normal utilization band. In Little's-Law terms this is the saturation regime — adding flow without expanding capacity will translate directly into queue length and lead time, not throughput. The reroute and capacity-rebalance actions in the right rail are the standard responses; the cascade-projection card shows which downstream nodes feel the pressure first.

A network-mode shift is visible: the operating regime changed enough to register as a structural break. In a logistics network this most often follows a single upstream incident that propagates downstream with measurable lag — the lag arcs in the system graph make the propagation explicit. The repair window is short; the next few hours of forward projection have the highest decision value.

The network is in a steady-throughput regime: the dominant dynamic is {motif_label}, with no saturated edges and no cascade signatures. Forecasts at multi-hour horizons are credible; this is the calibration window for tuning buffer levels and lead-time targets.
